newsitem.title: UK: FX industry upbeat on G20 clearing/settlement plan.
newsitem.headline: FX industry upbeat on G20 clearing/settlement plan.

text.p: Cooperation has broken out in the world of foreign exchange dealing between a group of major banks and two settlement providers. The result, say industry watchers, can only be good.

A group of major banks, known as the Group of 20 (G20), confirmed on Thursday it was in talks with London-based Exchange Clearing House (ECHO) and Multinet International Bank (Multinet) of the U.S. with a view towards creating an industry-owned venture for the reduction of foreign exchange settlement risk.

"What you have now is a clear way forward," said Graham Duncan, former chief executive of Echo and now consultant at London-based KM Partnership, a clearing, settlement and payment systems consultancy.

"The industry had a situation of a lot of apparently competing (clearing and settlement) solutions. A lot of people who were not yet committed to one route or another were having some difficulty in making up their minds because they weren't sure which one was going to last."
Thursday's confirmation the G20 would pursue development of a continuous linked settlement (CLS) system and the cooperation of the settlement providers goes some way to end that confusion.

"This is single industry utility," said Philip Lynch, chief executive of ECHO. "The benefit to the industry is that they'll be able to look at one solution and get involved with today's solution now and help be part of the ultimate solution, so to speak, of CLS."

CLS is a payment-versus-payment (PVP) system whereby forex transactions are routed through a central clearing bank and payments from one member are immediately offset by a matched payment from another.
This central clearer handles those currencies where domestic payment systems are in operation and between countries where such systems have overlapping hours.

The CLS system eliminates the so-called 'Herstatt risk', the risk of counterparty failure during the time lag between making a payment in one currency and receiving the second leg of the transaction. The current system can see delays for up to three days before being settled.

Settlement providers such as ECHO, in live operation for almost two years, and the soon-to-be-launched Multinet, lessen Herstatt risk by netting out gross payments and receivables into a single payment in or out for each member, but they do not eliminate it.

CLS does not necessarily need netting to achieve its goals -- gross payments can be settled just as easily as netted payments -- but the netting providers are seen adding experience to the G20 project as well as the versatility and added efficiency netting provides.
"Some may want to settle transactions net or gross, so CLS would have to be able to settle both," said Rob Close, programme director at G20 and payments strategy director at Barclays Bank.
"We have worked out how to settle gross or net and can do that very effectively. If we receive netted inputs that helps CLS, it helps to have a balance of both gross and netted inputs."

Domestic payment systems, such the Chips (Clearing House Interbank Payments System) in the U.S. and the UK's Chaps (Clearing House Automated Payments System), are currently the most efficient way of tranferring payments but even these can be susceptible to overloading or even breaking down.
Netted transactions, say supporters, can reduce the strain on CLS and underlying payment systems which can potentially see hundreds of thousands of transactions per day.
The commercial settlement providers can also augment CLS' reach by pre-settling currencies not covered by CLS.

The cooperation also eases some of the earlier concerns raised by Group of 40 (G40) banks, a group of 48 commercial and investment banks formed to establish cooperation to reduce forex settlement risk.
The G40 has in the past expressed concern over being distanced from CLS and, if it becomes an industry standard, being marginalised by CLS transaction costs.
However, it is envisaged that by pre-settling through ECHO or Multinet, payments through CLS will be reduced and, for some users, will actually be quite small.
"The idea is that it's not going to be a profit-maximising institution, it's something there that's covering its costs but doing no more than that," said one banker close to the project.

This cooperation comes hot on the heels of last year's Allsop report, the G10 group of leading central banks report on foreign exchange settlement risk giving market practitioners two years to find a solution.
The CLS project and the ECHO/Multinet cooperation is seen curbing the implied threat the G10 will find its own solution if the industry fails to do so.

"This was very much a spur to the market. The Allsop analysis highlighted that banks did not have suffient control of their settlement risk, that report was a real service to the industry," said KM Partnership's Duncan.
